method: Our values use pipeline/stats.py (Sen slope, persistence-adjusted Mann-Kendall interval) on the shipped data assets.

cases.title: Global warming rate, 1981-2025
cases.question: Does our global-mean temperature trend match NASA, NOAA and the Met Office?

our.label: MERRA-2 2 m air temperature (Sen slope, 95% CI persistence-adjusted)

reference.label: Range of GISTEMP v4, NOAAGlobalTemp and HadCRUT5 (same Sen method)

cases.rule: Pass if our trend lies inside the range spanned by the three reference indices; partial if outside it but same sign and within 25% of the nearest edge; fail otherwise.
cases.explanation: MERRA-2 shows clear warming in the same direction but its rate sits just outside the range of the three indices. Reference indices (Sen slope, deg C/decade): GISTEMP v4 0.211, NOAAGlobalTemp 0.200, HadCRUT 5.0.2.0 0.213. Not a like-for-like quantity: MERRA-2 T2M is air temperature over land and ocean from a reanalysis, while the indices blend land air and sea-surface temperature.

cases.title: Arctic amplification
cases.question: Is the Arctic warming about four times as fast as the whole planet?
cases.region: Arctic (north of 66.5 deg N) vs Whole Earth

our.label: MERRA-2 2 m temperature, ratio of OLS slopes (95% bootstrap interval)

cases.rule: Pass if our ratio is inside the published range 3.7 to 4.1; partial if outside it but within 25% of the nearest edge; fail otherwise.
cases.explanation: Our ratio shows strong Arctic amplification but lies outside the published 3.7 to 4.1 range. Our Arctic trend is 0.46 and global trend 0.15 deg C/decade (published: 0.73 and 0.19 over 1979-2021). The interval is a bootstrap over years. Caveats: our record starts in 1981, not 1979, and a reanalysis differs from the observational datasets used in the paper.

sources.citation: Rantanen, M. et al. (2022). The Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the globe since 1979. Communications Earth & Environment 3, 168

cases.title: De Bilt century warming vs KNMI
cases.question: Does the station record we ship show the century warming KNMI reports for De Bilt?

our.label: NCEI GSOM De Bilt annual mean temperature (Sen slope x 119 years, 95% CI persistence-adjusted)

cases.rule: Pass if our total rise is inside 2.0 to 2.5 deg C; partial if outside but within 15% of the nearest edge; fail otherwise.
cases.explanation: The NOAA station record for De Bilt gives the same century-scale warming that KNMI reports for the same station. Our trend is 0.169 deg C/decade over 120 valid years. KNMI states a total rise ("ruim 2" = a good 2 deg C) fitted by its own trend method; reading that as 2.0 to 2.5 deg C is our interpretation, and Sen's slope is not KNMI's method.

cases.rule: Pass if the two 95% intervals overlap and the slopes differ by at most 30% of the station slope; partial if the intervals overlap but the slopes differ by more; fail if the intervals do not overlap.

cases.title: India NO2 rise, 2005-2015
cases.question: Did tropospheric NO2 over northern India rise by more than half in a decade?

our.label: OMI NO2 (Sen slope x 10 years / 2005 level, 95% CI persistence-adjusted)

reference.label: Krotkov et al. 2016: India NO2 "more than 50 %"

cases.rule: Pass if our change is at least +50%; partial if it is between +25% and +50% (same sign, at least half the published size); fail otherwise.
cases.explanation: Our regional NO2 change does not show the published increase. Sen-line start value 1.66 x10^15 molec/cm2 in 2005; trend p (persistence-adjusted) = 0.016. Krotkov's abstract does not define its India region and its largest increases are at coal-power hotspots, so a whole-plain average is a diluted version of the same signal. Only 11 annual points are used, which is short.

sources.citation: Krotkov, N. A. et al. (2016). Aura OMI observations of regional SO2 and NO2 pollution changes from 2005 to 2015. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 16, 4605-4629
sources.quote: India's SO2 and NO2 levels are "increasing by more than 100 and 50 %, respectively, from 2005 to 2015." (abstract; the abstract does not define the India region).

sources.citation: NASA GES DISC, OMI/Aura NO2 Cloud-Screened Total and Tropospheric Column Daily L3 0.25 deg (OMNO2d v003), via Giovanni area averages

cases.title: Satellite-era ocean surface warming
cases.question: Does our sea-surface temperature trend fall in the range published for the satellite era?
cases.region: Global ocean box mean (ours) vs 60 deg S to 60 deg N (published)

our.label: NOAA OISST v2 (via KNMI Climate Explorer), Sen slope, 95% CI persistence-adjusted

reference.label: Menemenlis et al. 2025: four SST datasets span 0.108 to 0.184

cases.rule: Pass if our trend is inside 0.108 to 0.184 deg C/decade; partial if outside but same sign and within 25% of the nearest edge; fail otherwise.
cases.explanation: Our SST warming is positive and close to, but outside, the published spread of SST datasets. The published range is itself wide because SST datasets disagree with each other (that is the paper's point), so passing means 'plausible', not 'exact'. Differences in coverage: ours is a whole-globe box mean of OISST v2 for 1982-2022, theirs is 60 deg S to 60 deg N for 1982-2024.

sources.citation: Menemenlis, S., Vecchi, G. A., Yang, W., Fueglistaler, S., Raghuraman, S. P. (2025). Consequential differences in satellite-era sea surface temperature trends across datasets. Nature Climate Change 15, 897-903
sources.quote: "... trends in four widely used SST datasets show first-order differences, with 1982-2024 60° S to 60° N trends ranging from 0.108 to 0.184 °C per decade."

sources.citation: NOAA OISST v2 (Reynolds et al. 2002, J. Climate 15, 1609-1625), box mean via KNMI Climate Explorer

cases.title: Precipitation: MERRA-2 vs GPCP, 1981-2024
cases.question: Does the reanalysis precipitation trend agree with the gauge-satellite observational product?

our.label: MERRA-2 vs GPCP: regions with same-sign, overlapping trends

cases.rule: A region agrees if both datasets' Sen slopes have the same sign and their persistence-adjusted 95% intervals overlap. Pass if at least 75% of regions agree; partial if 50% to 75%; fail below 50%.
cases.explanation: MERRA-2 and GPCP agree in 10 of 17 regions; the rest differ in sign or have non-overlapping uncertainty. Median detrended year-to-year correlation across regions r = 0.54. Disagreeing regions: whole-earth, tropics, australian-outback, himalaya, indo-gangetic-plain, western-ghats, bengal-delta. Precipitation trends over 25 to 45 years carry wide intervals, so agreement is a lenient test; this check shows the datasets are consistent, not that either is exact.

cases.title: SeaWiFS chlorophyll near river mouths (challenge paper)
cases.question: Can we reproduce the coastal chlorophyll trends in the paper the challenge lists?
cases.region: Nine river-influenced coastal regions (paper) vs global ocean boxes (ours)
cases.period_reference: SeaWiFS era (study period not stated on the NTRS page)

reference.label: Acker et al. 2009: low-impact rivers show no significant trend; most human-impacted rivers show significant decreases (Pearl River increases)

cases.rule: Not scored. A check needs the same quantity in the same place: the paper's nine river-mouth boxes are not published as files, and our ocean chlorophyll series is the NOBM model, not SeaWiFS.
cases.explanation: We deliberately do not score this one. The paper analyses SeaWiFS satellite chlorophyll in nine small coastal boxes, where dissolved organic matter and sediment disturb the signal; our NOBM chlorophyll is a model product on coarse regional boxes that contain no river-mouth cells. Comparing them would produce a number with no meaning. What carries over is the lesson: coastal chlorophyll trends can reflect floods and water colour, not just phytoplankton, so we flag such series with cautions.

sources.citation: Acker, J. G., McMahon, E., Shen, S., Hearty, T., Casey, N. (2009). Time-Series Analysis of Remotely-Sensed SeaWiFS Chlorophyll in River-Influenced Coastal Regions. EARSeL eProceedings 8(2). NASA NTRS 20090042747
sources.quote: Nine river-influenced marine regions; "major river systems in regions with relatively low human impact showed no significant trends"; most systems with clear human impact showed significant negative trends, the exception being the Pearl River (positive). (paraphrased from the NTRS abstract; the page does not state the study period).
